terms.gloss: a robot: a machine that senses and moves by a program
evidence: M-O s.v. robot: robôtum, i (Egger D.L. 38)
Vicipaedia s.v. Catena cinematica: ATHLETE, robotum mobile JPL
terms.comment: The international word, from Czech robot (Čapek, 1920), made a neuter of the second declension. Morgan–Owens gives it from Egger and marks the second o long, as we write it; the Czech vowels are short, so the length is the source’s, and it puts the stress where most languages put it (ro-BŌ-tum). Vicipaedia uses the word as a common noun; it is weak evidence by itself. Preferred to the classical automatum because a robot is more than a self-moving contrivance, and because modern Latin also uses automatum of motor vehicles (see automaton).

terms.gloss: an automaton, a self-moving machine; of a robot, a modern use
evidence: Suet. Claud. 34.2: sī automatum vel pēgma vel quid tāle aliud parum cessisset
M-O s.v. machine: automatum, i n.
terms.comment: Greek αὐτόματον, with every vowel short. Classically a mechanical figure or stage device that moves by itself (Vitruvius, Petronius, Suetonius; Lewis & Short); used of a robot it is wider and older-sounding, and the case for it is that it is the classical word. See automaton.

robotum-o.html: Morgan–Owens prints robôtum, its circumflex marking a long vowel. The word is not in Lewis & Short, and the Czech robot has two short vowels: with a short o the Latin stress would fall on the first syllable (RO-bo-tum), as Czech has it. We follow the source; the choice is open to review.

phrases.latin: Hoc robōtum nōn ambulat, sed volvitur.
phrases.english: This robot doesn’t walk; it rolls.
The robot is cleaning the floor; lift your feet!

sources: Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.vv. machine; robot.
